briefing:
Day 20 ends with the Suwalki Gap Crisis at its most promising diplomatic moment. Every major obstacle to Istanbul II has been cleared: Russia has accepted IAEA Smolensk access (resolving the warhead discrepancy), the summit format has been agreed (three-layer structure satisfying all parties), gas deliveries have increased to 25%, and markets are rallying strongly. The summit begins TOMORROW.

The three-layer Istanbul format represents a genuine diplomatic innovation: Trump gets his bilateral Putin meeting, the European Three get their formal seat, and frontline states get voice without veto. This structure was designed to prevent any single party from blocking progress while ensuring all stakeholders feel heard.

Military posture remains completely stable. No combat. All forces in garrison. Several NATO allies again proposed new forward deployments — ALL REJECTED by GM due to war support constraints (US 14%, GB 19%, FR 9%, all well below 50%). The alliance's military posture is frozen; only diplomatic solutions are politically viable.

Hungary's political crisis has reached terminal velocity — 13 Fidesz defectors, Constitutional Court hearing on Day 23, Orban's majority collapsed below functional threshold. The regime appears to be in its final days.

Three questions for Istanbul II (Day 21-22): (1) Will Russia's Kaliningrad 40% drawdown proposal survive NATO scrutiny, or will allies demand more? (2) Can the sanctions-benchmarks framework satisfy both Russian need for relief and NATO need for verified compliance? (3) Will the IAEA Smolensk verification on Day 22 confirm Russia's account or expose new discrepancies?
narrative:
Day 20 — the eve of Istanbul II — produces the final diplomatic breakthrough needed for the summit to succeed: Russia formally accepts IAEA access to the Smolensk Oblast storage facility where it claims the two missing warheads were relocated. The announcement comes at 14:00 CET through the Russian permanent mission to the IAEA in Vienna, and within minutes markets surge and diplomatic channels light up. IAEA Director General Grossi confirms that a three-person verification team will travel to Smolensk on Day 22, concurrent with Istanbul II, ensuring that nuclear accountability proceeds in parallel with political negotiations.

The Istanbul II format dispute — the most intense transatlantic disagreement of the crisis — is resolved through a compromise brokered by Turkish FM Fidan in a marathon series of phone calls. The summit will have a three-layer structure: (1) a Trump-Putin bilateral opening session on Day 21 morning, covering nuclear verification and the warhead issue; (2) an expanded 'Istanbul Format' session in the afternoon including the European Three (UK-FR-DE) plus Turkey, covering Kaliningrad, sanctions framework, and European security architecture; (3) a concluding plenary on Day 22 open to all affected nations (Poland, Baltics, and other NATO allies as observers with speaking rights). This 'Istanbul Three-Layer' format gives Trump his bilateral prestige, gives the European Three their seat at the table, and gives frontline states voice without veto. It is immediately accepted by all parties.

Russia also increases gas deliveries to 25% of pre-crisis baseline (up from 15%), framed as a 'pre-summit goodwill gesture.' European gas futures drop another 5%. Combined with the Smolensk access announcement, markets post their strongest session since before the crisis — oil drops to $77, the DAX closes at pre-crisis levels, and the ruble strengthens to 120/USD. For the first time in 20 days, the economic trajectory is clearly positive.

In Budapest, the Orban regime enters its final spiral. Three more Fidesz MPs publicly join Magyar's call for resignation, bringing the total defectors to 13. Orban's theoretical majority is now 119-80 — well below the 100-vote threshold for parliamentary function. The Constitutional Court announces it will hear Magyar's petition for a declaration of 'governance incapacity' on Day 23. Orban, still at his Felcsut estate, makes no public statement. His press secretary reads a single line: 'The Prime Minister is preparing for the new political season.' European observers interpret this as preparation for resignation.

surprises: At 16:30 CET, Turkish Intelligence (MIT) Director Ibrahim Kalin places a call to IAEA Director General Grossi with an extraordinary proposal: Turkey offers to host the two missing warheads in temporary IAEA-supervised custody at the Incirlik Air Base — the same facility where the S-400 systems were transferred to US custody weeks earlier. The proposal would allow Russia to 'return' the warheads to international supervision without the humiliation of having them confiscated, and would give IAEA physical custody for verification before their return to Russia. Grossi describes the proposal as 'creative and worth exploring.' If accepted, it would resolve the warhead crisis in a single stroke — but it requires both Russia and the US to agree to Turkish custody of Russian nuclear weapons on a NATO base. The diplomatic complexity is staggering, but the logic is elegant.

In a secure video call at 21:00 CET, Orban's chief of staff Janos Lazar contacts the German Ambassador to Hungary and asks a single question: 'If the Prime Minister were to resign, would the European Union be prepared to immediately release the frozen cohesion funds to a successor government?' The German Ambassador, stunned, replies that this would need to be discussed with Brussels but that 'a new government committed to the rule of law would find the EU responsive.' Lazar says 'Thank you' and hangs up. Within hours, German intelligence reports the call to Berlin, and the European Council President is briefed. The interpretation is unanimous: Orban is exploring his exit.
